Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Diego had always been drawn to the methodical world of engineering, where problems could be solved with precision and predictability. As a QA engineer at a tech firm in San Francisco's Mission District, he spent his days testing software and identifying glitches. But on a typical Wednesday evening two years ago, Diego's life was forever altered when a devastating fire broke out at the Ghost Ship warehouse party in Oakland. He had been attending the event with friends from college, and as they tried to escape the inferno, Diego became separated from them in the chaos. The memory of that night still felt like an open wound. Diego recalled the deafening roar of the flames, the crushing heat, and the desperate screams for help. What haunted him most was the image of his friend, Alex, who had been right behind him as they fled, but never made it out. The police investigation later revealed that a combination of factors, including electrical issues and inadequate safety measures, contributed to the tragedy. In the months following the disaster, Diego found himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. He stopped attending social gatherings, fearing that conversations might turn to accidents or tragedies like Ghost Ship. Even casual discussions about car crashes or plane accidents would send his mind spiraling back to that terrible night. The mere mention of such topics made him feel detached and unreal, as if he was observing the world around him from a distant, numb place. Diego began to avoid watching TV programs or films that depicted similar events, fearing they would trigger another wave of memories and emotions. He also stopped following news outlets on social media, unable to bear the constant stream of updates about accidents and disasters. His avoidance behaviors extended to encounters with police officers; seeing them in uniform made him anxious, reminding him of the investigation and the sense of helplessness he felt during those long days after the fire. As Diego's avoidance strategies became more entrenched, his mind began to wander into dark territories. He found himself ruminating on counterfactual scenarios, wondering what would have happened if they had left the party earlier or taken a different exit route. These thoughts often led him down a rabbit hole of self-blame and guilt, as he tormented himself with the idea that he should have protected his friends and failed to do so. The fear of harm became an ever-present companion, making Diego question the reliability of strangers and the safety of public spaces. He started to see the world as a treacherous place, where danger lurked around every corner. His sense of hopelessness deepened, as he came to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore – that some fundamental aspect of his life had been irreparably damaged. At work, Diego's performance began to suffer. He found it increasingly difficult to focus on testing software when his mind was consumed by these thoughts. His colleagues noticed a change in him and grew concerned, but Diego pushed them away, fearing that opening up about his experiences would only lead to more pain. It wasn't until recently, after a particularly grueling argument with a friend who had tried to stage an intervention, that Diego realized he needed help. The weight of his emotions had become too crushing to bear alone. He was afraid that seeking therapy might force him to confront the trauma head-on, but he knew he couldn't continue living in this state of constant dread and avoidance. As he sat in his small apartment, surrounded by the familiar comforts of code and circuitry, Diego felt a glimmer of hope – perhaps, just perhaps, there was a way to rebuild his life, one carefully crafted step at a time.
